hints: Differentiate $x=te^{2t}$ with the product rule and differentiate $y=t^2+t+3$ directly.
Factor $dx/dt$ as $e^{2t}(1+2t)$ before cancelling the common factor with $dy/dt$.
walkthrough:
Differentiate $x = t\mathrm{e}^{2t}$ with respect to $t$ using the product rule, $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(uv) = u'v + uv'$:
$$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t} = (1)\mathrm{e}^{2t} + t(2\mathrm{e}^{2t}) = \mathrm{e}^{2t}(1 + 2t)$$

Differentiate $y = t^2 + t + 3$ with respect to $t$:
$$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t} = 2t + 1$$

Apply the chain rule for parametric differentiation:
$$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \dfrac{\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}}{\dfrac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}} = \dfrac{2t + 1}{\mathrm{e}^{2t}(1 + 2t)}$$

Cancel the common factor $(2t + 1) = (1 + 2t)$ from numerator and denominator:
$$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \dfrac{1}{\mathrm{e}^{2t}} = \mathrm{e}^{-2t}$$

ai_rubric.Differentiating Parametric Curves: Derives $dx/dt=e^{2t}+2te^{2t}$. With $dy/dt=2t+1$, deriving $dy/dx=e^{-2t}$. The final result is $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=e^{-2t}$.

hints: At $t=-1$, first find the point on the curve and evaluate the tangent gradient $e^{-2t}$.
The normal gradient is the negative reciprocal of the tangent gradient.
Form the normal through the point found at $t=-1$, then set $x=0$ and simplify its $y$-coordinate exactly.
walkthrough:
Calculate the coordinates of the point on the curve at parameter $t = -1$:
$$x = (-1)\mathrm{e}^{2(-1)} = -\mathrm{e}^{-2}$$
$$y = (-1)^2 + (-1) + 3 = 1 - 1 + 3 = 3$$
The point of contact is $(-\mathrm{e}^{-2}, 3)$.

Evaluate the gradient of the tangent at $t = -1$:
$$m_{\text{tangent}} = \mathrm{e}^{-2(-1)} = \mathrm{e}^2$$

Find the gradient of the normal to the curve, which is the negative reciprocal of the tangent gradient:
$$m_{\text{normal}} = -\dfrac{1}{m_{\text{tangent}}} = -\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{e}^2} = -\mathrm{e}^{-2}$$

Write the equation of the normal line passing through $(-\mathrm{e}^{-2}, 3)$ with gradient $-\mathrm{e}^{-2}$:
$$y - y_1 = m_{\text{normal}}(x - x_1)$$
$$y - 3 = -\mathrm{e}^{-2}(x - (-\mathrm{e}^{-2}))$$
$$y - 3 = -\mathrm{e}^{-2}(x + \mathrm{e}^{-2})$$

Substitute $x = 0$ into the normal equation to find its $y$-intercept:
$$y - 3 = -\mathrm{e}^{-2}(0 + \mathrm{e}^{-2})$$
$$y - 3 = -\mathrm{e}^{-2}\cdot\mathrm{e}^{-2} = -\mathrm{e}^{-4}$$
$$y = 3 - \mathrm{e}^{-4}$$
Conclude that the normal line passes through the point $(0, 3 - \mathrm{e}^{-4})$ as required.

ai_rubric.Finding Equations of Normals: Derives $x=-e^{-2}$ and $y=3$ at $t=-1$. Derives gradient of the normal $=-e^{-2}$. The normal is $y-3=-e^{-2}(x+e^{-2})$, so at $x=0$, $y=3-e^{-4}$.
